name: Nova-C

solarArrayW.note: Intuitive Machines' Nova-C release (2019, reposted by collectSPACE): "At least 200 watts of power on the surface" — used as the conservative value (astronomy.com, 2025: three panels "afford 200 watts"). Upper bound: the FCC IM-1 application gives "a maximum of 788 W" for the three fixed panels; if that is their summed rating, our normalisation (output at the best polar Sun direction) would give ~490 W. Compare with the SOLAR what-if.

panels.note: Team description: 3 fixed panels (FCC IM-1 application confirms three fixed body-mounted solar panels; their directions are not published), 1 on the top deck and 2 on side walls of the hexagonal body, no Sun tracking (tip-overs of IM-1 and IM-2 cut their power). astronomy.com (2025): "one on the lander's top deck, plus two body-mounted arrays". Assumed: the two walls are adjacent (60° apart) and the 3 panels share the output equally.

batteryWh.note: FCC IM-1 application: three fixed body-mounted solar panels, Li-ion batteries with a total energy capacity of 1554 Wh, 28 VDC bus (ODAR: three 518 Wh battery assemblies). Replaces the earlier 700 Wh derived from 25 Ah × 28 V (secondary sources).

batteryRoundTripEff.note: Li-ion class value, not published for this lander: energy out / energy in of the cells. LLNL LEO tests (Mayer, Feikert, Kaschmitter): 86% called very good, 91% at 30% depth of discharge. Split evenly between charge and discharge (sqrt 0.9 each); power-electronics losses not included.

survivalLoadW.note: 1554 Wh / ~15 h (IM: comms 10–20 h after sunset)

designedForNight.note: battery limits — cannot survive lunar night

landingAccuracyM.note: Radius of the landing ellipse the verdict is re-checked over. IM-2 Athena (6 Mar 2025, Mons Mouton) landed more than 400 m from its target according to NASA (Intuitive Machines: 250 m); IM-1 (Feb 2024) came down ~1.5 km off after a laser rangefinder failure.

modelNote: Visualisation only. Bounding-box height scaled to 3.94 m: FCC IM-1 application gives Nova-C as 2.19 m × 2.385 m × 3.938 m (https://apps.fcc.gov/els/GetAtt.html?amp=&id=266519&x=). modelNozzleOffsetM: engine plume origin above the feet, visual estimate from the model's shape.

name: Blue Ghost

solarArrayW.note: Blue Ghost Mission 1: two side panels and one top-deck panel "provide up to 400 W" (Firefly). The 650 W in Wikipedia's infobox has no citation and is not used; Firefly's Blue Ghost product page lists > 400 W of payload power for later missions.

panels.note: Team description: 3 fixed panels on the top deck and the side walls, at different angles, powering the lander from sunrise to sunset without rotating mechanisms (Blue Ghost M1). Assumed: the side panels face opposite directions and the 3 panels share the output equally.

batteryWh.note: survivalLoadW × ~5 h night ops observed on M1

batteryRoundTripEff.note: Li-ion class value, not published for this lander: energy out / energy in of the cells. LLNL LEO tests (Mayer, Feikert, Kaschmitter): 86% called very good, 91% at 30% depth of discharge. Split evenly between charge and discharge (sqrt 0.9 each); power-electronics losses not included.

missionDurationDays.note: M1: 14+ days daylight + ~5 h into night

designedForNight.note: M1 configuration ended ~5 h after sunset

landingAccuracyM.note: Radius of the landing ellipse the verdict is re-checked over. Blue Ghost Mission 1 (2 Mar 2025) touched down within its 100 m landing target in Mare Crisium.

modelNote: Visualisation only. Approximate visual size: the model's bounding-box height is scaled to 2 m (team value). modelNozzleOffsetM: engine plume origin above the feet, visual estimate from the model's shape.

name: Griffin

solarArrayW.note: Class estimate: output not published. Astrobotic Lunar Landers PUG (2021) p. 28: Griffin "is designed to be power positive" on the surface (so the array must exceed the ~700 W day load) and "can be configured to carry larger solar arrays" than Peregrine.

panels.note: Team description: one large fixed panel on one side, optimised for polar missions; the lander yaws before touchdown so the panel faces the Sun. Astrobotic Lunar Landers PUG (2021) pp. 24, 28: polar missions "utilize side-mounted panels" (the Griffin Mission One configuration). Assumed: one vertical panel carries the whole output (count, size and tilt not published).

batteryRoundTripEff.note: Li-ion class value, not published for this lander: energy out / energy in of the cells. LLNL LEO tests (Mayer, Feikert, Kaschmitter): 86% called very good, 91% at 30% depth of discharge. Split evenly between charge and discharge (sqrt 0.9 each); power-electronics losses not included.

dayLoadW.note: Payload power from the Astrobotic Lunar Landers PUG (2021) p. 55: NOMINAL 1.0 W per kg of payload (PEAK 2.5 W/kg as scheduled) × 625 kg polar capacity (p. 24) = 625 W, plus ~75 W for the lander bus (assumption, not published).

missionDurationDays.note: Astrobotic Lunar Landers PUG (2021) p. 24, polar configuration: "Surface Operations Duration Up to 14 Days".

landingAccuracyM.note: Radius of the landing ellipse the verdict is re-checked over. Griffin has not landed yet; assumed between the results CLPS landers have demonstrated (Blue Ghost 100 m, Nova-C IM-2 400 m).

modelCredit: Model: concept image Meshy AI · 3D Microsoft TRELLIS.2 (MIT) · stylized, not manufacturer CAD
modelNote: Visualisation only. APPROXIMATE: the model's largest horizontal extent is scaled to 4.5 m.
